Title: Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1503
AnswerDetails: Real title: Mona Lisa (La Gioconda), Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1503-1519, Louvre, Paris. Trivia: it was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, a former museum workman, and the two years it spent missing are much of the reason it is the most famous painting in the world.

Title: Sandro Botticelli, c. 1485
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Birth of Venus, Sandro Botticelli, c. 1485, Uffizi, Florence. Trivia: Botticelli painted it on canvas at a time when Florentine works on this scale were normally painted on wooden panel.

Title: Michelangelo, 1508-1512
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Creation of Adam, Michelangelo, c. 1512, Sistine Chapel, Vatican City. Trivia: The nearly touching hands occupy only a small part of the vast Sistine Chapel ceiling, yet became one of art history’s most reproduced details.

Title: Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1495-1498
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Last Supper, Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1495-1498, Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. Trivia: Leonardo painted it with an experimental wall technique rather than true fresco, which caused deterioration to begin within decades.

Title: Raphael, 1509-1511
AnswerDetails: Real title: The School of Athens, Raphael, 1509-1511, Apostolic Palace, Vatican City. Trivia: Raphael gathered ancient philosophers into an imaginary architecture and gave several figures the faces of Renaissance contemporaries.

Title: Jan van Eyck, 1434
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Arnolfini Portrait, Jan van Eyck, 1434, National Gallery, London. Trivia: The convex mirror reflects two additional people entering the room and is surrounded by tiny scenes from the Passion of Christ.

Title: Hieronymus Bosch, c. 1490-1510
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Garden of Earthly Delights, Hieronymus Bosch, c. 1490-1510, Museo del Prado, Madrid. Trivia: When its wings close, the triptych shows the world as a fragile transparent sphere during Creation.

Title: Hans Holbein the Younger, 1533
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Ambassadors, Hans Holbein the Younger, 1533, National Gallery, London. Trivia: The strange diagonal shape across the floor resolves into a skull when viewed from a sharp angle, a feat of anamorphosis.

Title: Sandro Botticelli, c. 1480
AnswerDetails: Real title: Primavera (Spring), Sandro Botticelli, c. 1480, Uffizi, Florence. Trivia: botanists have identified around 200 different plant species in its meadow.

Title: Vincent van Gogh, 1889
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Starry Night, Vincent van Gogh, 1889, Museum of Modern Art, New York. Trivia: van Gogh painted it from the window of his room at the Saint-Paul asylum in Saint-Remy-de-Provence, where he had admitted himself voluntarily the year before.

Title: Georges Seurat, 1884
AnswerDetails: Real title: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, Georges Seurat, 1884-1886, Art Institute of Chicago. Trivia: Seurat worked on it for about two years and made dozens of preparatory studies, then later added a painted border of dots so the picture would not have to sit against a conventional frame.

Title: Claude Monet, 1872
AnswerDetails: Real title: Impression, Sunrise, Claude Monet, 1872, Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris. Trivia: A critic mocked its title in 1874 and inadvertently supplied the Impressionists with the name that endured.

Title: Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1876
AnswerDetails: Real title: Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1876, Musée d’Orsay, Paris. Trivia: Renoir painted friends and models among the Sunday crowd at a popular Montmartre dance garden.

Title: Édouard Manet, 1882
AnswerDetails: Real title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, Édouard Manet, 1882, Courtauld Gallery, London. Trivia: The mirror’s seemingly inconsistent reflection has generated debate about the positions of the barmaid, customer, and viewer.

Title: Edgar Degas, c. 1874
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Ballet Class, Edgar Degas, c. 1874, Musée d’Orsay, Paris. Trivia: The celebrated choreographer Jules Perrot stands at center while dancers stretch, scratch, and wait rather than perform.

Title: Claude Monet, 1875
AnswerDetails: Real title: Woman with a Parasol – Madame Monet and Her Son, Claude Monet, 1875, National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.. Trivia: Monet painted the low viewpoint and windblown veil outdoors, giving the portrait the spontaneity of a passing moment.

Title: Vincent van Gogh, 1888
AnswerDetails: Real title: Café Terrace at Night, Vincent van Gogh, 1888, Kröller-Müller Museum, Otterlo. Trivia: It was among van Gogh’s first paintings to feature a star-filled night sky, made months before The Starry Night.

Title: Vincent van Gogh, 1888
AnswerDetails: Real title: Sunflowers, Vincent van Gogh, 1888, National Gallery, London. Trivia: Van Gogh painted the Arles sunflowers to decorate the Yellow House before Paul Gauguin arrived to stay.

Title: Paul Cézanne, c. 1890-1895
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Card Players, Paul Cézanne, c. 1890-1895, Musée d’Orsay, Paris. Trivia: Cézanne made five painted versions, progressively reducing the cast and stripping away narrative detail.

Title: Gustave Caillebotte, 1877
AnswerDetails: Real title: Paris Street; Rainy Day (Rue de Paris, temps de pluie), Gustave Caillebotte, 1877, Art Institute of Chicago. Trivia: the crossing is today's Place de Dublin in Paris's eighth arrondissement, in the city Haussmann had just rebuilt. It was praised for its precision at the Third Impressionist Exhibition in 1877, then spent decades out of sight with the painter's family; the Art Institute bought it in 1964, and that purchase helped revive Caillebotte's reputation.

Title: Hasegawa Tōhaku, c. 1595
AnswerDetails: Real title: Pine Trees (Shōrin-zu byōbu), Hasegawa Tōhaku, c. 1595, Tokyo National Museum. Trivia: it is a pair of six-panel folding screens in ink on paper, pines half lost in mist, an expression of ma, the Japanese idea of meaningful empty space. They are said to be the first paintings of their size to show nothing but trees, and were named a National Treasure of Japan in 1952.

Title: Johannes Vermeer, c. 1665
AnswerDetails: Real title: Girl with a Pearl Earring, Johannes Vermeer, c. 1665, Mauritshuis, The Hague. Trivia: it is not a portrait but a tronie - a study of a type or a costume rather than of a named sitter - so nobody knows who she was, or whether she was anyone at all.

Title: Rembrandt van Rijn, 1642
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Night Watch (Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq), Rembrandt van Rijn, 1642, Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Trivia: it is not a night scene - darkened varnish earned it that nickname - and in 1715 it was cut down on all four sides to fit a wall in Amsterdam's town hall, losing two figures from the left edge.

Title: Caravaggio, 1599-1600
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Calling of Saint Matthew, Caravaggio, 1599-1600, San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome. Trivia: A narrow beam of light follows Christ’s pointing hand into a room dressed in Caravaggio’s own contemporary fashion.

Title: Artemisia Gentileschi, c. 1612-1613
AnswerDetails: Real title: Judith Slaying Holofernes, Artemisia Gentileschi, c. 1612-1613, Museo di Capodimonte, Naples. Trivia: Gentileschi returned to the Judith story several times and made its physical struggle unusually forceful for the period.

Title: Diego Velázquez, 1656
AnswerDetails: Real title: Las Meninas, Diego Velázquez, 1656, Museo del Prado, Madrid. Trivia: A mirror at the back reflects the king and queen, complicating where they—and the viewer—stand in the scene.

Title: Rembrandt van Rijn, 1632
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp, Rembrandt van Rijn, 1632, Mauritshuis, The Hague. Trivia: The painting was a commissioned group portrait, yet Rembrandt turned the sitters into participants in a dramatic public dissection.

Title: Johannes Vermeer, c. 1658-1660
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Milkmaid, Johannes Vermeer, c. 1658-1660, Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Trivia: Vermeer used tiny dots of bright paint on the bread and basket to make light seem to sparkle across their surfaces.

Title: Johannes Vermeer, c. 1660
AnswerDetails: Real title: View of Delft, Johannes Vermeer, c. 1660-1661, Mauritshuis, The Hague. Trivia: Proust called it the most beautiful painting in the world - in his novel, the writer Bergotte dies in front of its "little patch of yellow wall".

Title: Jean-Honoré Fragonard, 1767
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Swing, Jean-Honoré Fragonard, 1767, Wallace Collection, London. Trivia: A hidden admirer looks up the young woman’s dress while an older man, unaware of the joke, pushes the swing.

Title: Jacques-Louis David, 1784
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Oath of the Horatii, Jacques-Louis David, 1784, Louvre, Paris. Trivia: Its rigid male figures and grieving women became a textbook contrast between civic duty and private sorrow.

Title: Thomas Gainsborough, c. 1770
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Blue Boy, Thomas Gainsborough, c. 1770, The Huntington, San Marino, California. Trivia: nobody is sure who the boy is. He was long said to be Jonathan Buttall, a hardware merchant's son, but is more likely Gainsborough's nephew, Gainsborough Dupont, and the 17th-century costume is a homage to van Dyck. When it was sold to Henry Huntington in 1921, 90,000 people went to see it at the National Gallery in London before it left for California.

Title: Edvard Munch, 1893
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Scream, Edvard Munch, 1893, National Museum, Oslo. Trivia: the figure is not the one screaming. Munch's own note describes hearing a scream passing through nature and covering his ears against it. He made several versions, in paint and in pastel, plus a lithograph.

Title: Gustav Klimt, 1908
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Kiss (Der Kuss), Gustav Klimt, 1907-1908, Belvedere, Vienna. Trivia: the gold leaf belongs to Klimt's golden phase, which followed a trip to Ravenna and its Byzantine mosaics.

Title: Arnold Böcklin, 1883
AnswerDetails: Real title: Isle of the Dead, Arnold Böcklin, 1883, Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin. Trivia: Böcklin painted five versions of the haunting island; the third became especially famous through reproductions.

Title: Wassily Kandinsky, 1913
AnswerDetails: Real title: Composition VII, Wassily Kandinsky, 1913, Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow. Trivia: often called the most complex picture he ever made - months of studies, then the canvas itself painted in under four days.

Title: Franz Marc, 1911
AnswerDetails: Real title: Blue Horse I, Franz Marc, 1911, Lenbachhaus, Munich. Trivia: Marc associated blue with spirituality and masculinity and repeatedly used animals to imagine a purer world.

Title: Wassily Kandinsky, 1923
AnswerDetails: Real title: Composition 8, Wassily Kandinsky, 1923, Guggenheim, New York. Trivia: Kandinsky prized it above the stormier Composition 7 - he saw the circle, not the storm, as the high point of his postwar work.

Title: Gustav Klimt, 1907
AnswerDetails: Real title: Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I, Gustav Klimt, 1907, Neue Galerie, New York. Trivia: seized by the Nazis, recovered by Adele's niece Maria Altmann in a landmark 2006 restitution case, and sold for a then-record $135 million - the story behind the film Woman in Gold.

Title: Egon Schiele, 1912
AnswerDetails: Real title: Self-Portrait with Physalis, Egon Schiele, 1912, Leopold Museum, Vienna. Trivia: the physalis is the papery Chinese-lantern plant, and Schiele painted a matching portrait of Wally Neuzil as its companion.

Title: Henri Rousseau, 1891
AnswerDetails: Real title: Tiger in a Tropical Storm (Surprised!), Henri Rousseau, 1891, National Gallery, London. Trivia: Rousseau never left France - his jungles came from Paris hothouses, zoos and picture books.

Title: Piet Mondrian, 1930
AnswerDetails: Real title: Composition II in Red, Blue, and Yellow, Piet Mondrian, 1930, Kunsthaus Zürich. Trivia: Mondrian varied the widths of black lines and the sizes of color blocks to make an asymmetrical image feel balanced.

Title: Caspar David Friedrich, c. 1818
AnswerDetails: Real title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, Caspar David Friedrich, c. 1818, Kunsthalle Hamburg. Trivia: the hidden face is the point. Friedrich's Ruckenfigur device puts the viewer in the man's place looking out, and who he was meant to be has never been settled.

Title: Eugène Delacroix, 1830
AnswerDetails: Real title: Liberty Leading the People, Eugène Delacroix, 1830, Louvre, Paris. Trivia: The allegorical Liberty carries the tricolor beside recognizable contemporary Parisians, blending myth with eyewitness politics.

Title: Théodore Géricault, 1818-1819
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Raft of the Medusa, Théodore Géricault, 1818-1819, Louvre, Paris. Trivia: Géricault interviewed survivors and studied corpses to depict the aftermath of a notorious French naval disaster.

Title: J. M. W. Turner, 1844
AnswerDetails: Real title: Snow Storm: Steam-Boat off a Harbour’s Mouth, J. M. W. Turner, 1842, Tate Britain, London. Trivia: Turner helped spread the story that he had himself tied to a ship’s mast in a storm, though historians doubt it happened.

Title: Gustave Courbet, 1849-1850
AnswerDetails: Real title: A Burial at Ornans, Gustave Courbet, 1849-1850, Musée d’Orsay, Paris. Trivia: Courbet gave a provincial funeral the enormous scale traditionally reserved for history painting.

Title: Jean-François Millet, 1857
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Gleaners, Jean-François Millet, 1857, Musée d’Orsay, Paris. Trivia: The women collect scraps left after harvest, a humble act that made prosperous viewers uneasy in the politically tense 1850s.

Title: James McNeill Whistler, 1871
AnswerDetails: Real title: Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, James McNeill Whistler, 1871, Musée d’Orsay, Paris. Trivia: Better known as Whistler’s Mother, it was conceived as an arrangement of tones rather than a sentimental family portrait.

Title: Grant Wood, 1930
AnswerDetails: Real title: American Gothic, Grant Wood, 1930, Art Institute of Chicago. Trivia: The models were Wood’s sister and his dentist, posed as types rather than as a married farm couple.

Title: Edward Hopper, 1942
AnswerDetails: Real title: Nighthawks, Edward Hopper, 1942, Art Institute of Chicago. Trivia: Hopper said the setting was inspired by a restaurant on New York’s Greenwich Avenue, but the exact site remains uncertain.

Title: Emanuel Leutze, 1851
AnswerDetails: Real title: Washington Crossing the Delaware, Emanuel Leutze, 1851, Metropolitan Museum of Art. Trivia: painted in Germany with the Rhine standing in for the Delaware; the first version was destroyed in a British air raid in 1942.

Title: Frederic Edwin Church, 1859
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Heart of the Andes, Frederic Edwin Church, 1859, Metropolitan Museum of Art. Trivia: at its debut, visitors paid 25 cents and were handed opera glasses to explore the detail.

Title: Winslow Homer, 1876
AnswerDetails: Real title: Breezing Up (A Fair Wind), Winslow Homer, 1873-1876, National Gallery of Art, Washington. Trivia: Homer reworked it for three years and showed it at the 1876 centennial, where it was celebrated as an image of the young country's optimism.

Title: Mary Cassatt, 1893
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Child's Bath, Mary Cassatt, 1893, Art Institute of Chicago. Trivia: the tipped-up floor and cropped view come straight from the Japanese prints Cassatt collected.

Title: John Singer Sargent, 1884
AnswerDetails: Real title: Madame X (Madame Pierre Gautreau), John Singer Sargent, 1884, Metropolitan Museum of Art. Trivia: the original showed a fallen shoulder strap and the scandal drove Sargent from Paris - he repainted the strap and later called it the best thing he had done.

Title: Henry Fuseli, 1781
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Nightmare, Henry Fuseli, 1781, Detroit Institute of Arts. Trivia: a reproduction of it hung in Freud's waiting room, and Fuseli painted several more versions after the first became a sensation.

Title: Henri Rousseau, 1910
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Dream, Henri Rousseau, 1910, MoMA, New York. Trivia: painted months before his death; the sofa in the jungle drew mockery until Picasso and the avant-garde championed him.

Title: Francisco de Goya, c. 1820
AnswerDetails: Real title: Saturn Devouring His Son, Francisco de Goya, c. 1820-1823, Prado, Madrid. Trivia: one of the Black Paintings Goya made directly on the walls of his own house - never meant to be exhibited at all.

Title: William Blake, c. 1805
AnswerDetails: Real title: The Great Red Dragon and the Woman Clothed in Sun, William Blake, c. 1805-1810. Trivia: one of a series of biblical watercolours, made famous again by the novel and films of Red Dragon.
